title: Evaluating the Multilingual Capabilities of LLM-based Web UI Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>The emergence of Large Language Model (LLM) based agents represents a paradigm shift in artificial intelligence, enabling autonomous systems capable of planning, reasoning, tool utilization, and memory maintenance while interacting with dynamic environments. As these agents become increasingly sophisticated and are deployed in real-world applications, the need for comprehensive and rigorous evaluation methodologies has become paramount. This paper provides a systematic survey of evaluation methodologies for LLM-based agents, examining benchmarks and frameworks across four critical dimensions: fundamental agent capabilities (planning, tool use, self-reflection, and memory), application-specific benchmarks (web agents, software engineering agents, scientific agents, and conversational agents), generalist agent evaluation frameworks, and emerging multi-agent system assessment approaches. We analyze the strengths and limitations of current evaluation practices, identify critical gaps in cost-efficiency assessment, safety evaluation, and robustness testing, and propose future research directions to address these challenges. Our analysis reveals that while significant progress has been made in developing evaluation frameworks, substantial work remains to establish standardized, scalable, and reliable assessment methodologies for LLM agents operating in complex, real-world scenarios.</jats:p>
title: The State of Evaluating LLM Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>This treatise conducts an evaluation of OpenClaw, an artificial intelligence agent grounded in large language models (LLMs), from a user-centered perspective through a light-weight real-world experiment. The study is designed to analyze the system's behavior under different categories of tasks, including benign, risk-sensitive, and adversarial scenarios. The results demonstrate that OpenClaw shows dependable working capability in ordinary tasks, producing structured and accurate outputs, while also exhibiting a certain level of basic safety awareness in adversarial situations such as prompt injection and harmful command requests. However, limitations become apparent when users encounter risk-sensitive situations. The system may still generate potentially dangerous outputs, even when warnings are provided, indicating that its safety mechanisms rely more on notification rather than strict prevention. In addition, the behavior of the system is found to vary depending on how user inputs are phrased, revealing sensitivity to prompt formulation. These findings suggest that, although OpenClaw has practical usability as a general-purpose assistant, there remains a clear need for stronger and more reliable safety control mechanisms in LLM-based agents to ensure secure real-world deployment.</jats:p>
title: Evaluating the Safety of LLM-Based Agents: A User-Centered Study of OpenClaw
